File → New Project… → Empty project. The floor is a grid, 1600 × 520 px to start; Floor on the simulator toolbar makes it 2400 × 600, 3200 × 700 or 4000 × 800, and it grows headroom by itself when a tall part sits near its top edge. One pixel is 1/60 of a metre in the 3D view, so a 20 m conveyor is 1200 px and the main line of Part IV runs most of the floor.

Placing and arranging

In Program mode open the Palette drawer, click a part, click the floor: it is placed, named (PE_1, Belt_2…) and wired, every signal taking the next free point of the right kind. Hold Shift while clicking to place several. Drag to move: parts snap to the grid, conveyors snap end to end and line up, and a sensor or station dragged near a conveyor snaps onto its centreline and takes its rotation. R rotates the selected part; the Properties drawer has Rotation and Position fields for exact placement, and the arrow keys nudge. Ctrl+click selects several; right-click (or long-press on a touch screen) for Duplicate, Delete, Group, Rotate and Put on a Panel. The floor is locked while the controller runs: in Run mode a click operates a button or a switch instead of moving it, and View → Lock Parts in Place keeps it that way in Program mode too.

Properties

Click a part and the Properties drawer shows its name (edit it there; its alias tags and every rung that uses them follow), rotation and position, the name-tag setting, its settings (the parameters listed in chapter 13) and Signals and Addresses: every signal, its kind, its point and the alias it has. With nothing selected the drawer is the Scene sheet: the view, the floor, the background, how many points of each kind are in use, Alias all I/O, Clear Parts and Reset Sim.

Panels

A Panel / Enclosure is a drawn operator station. Drop buttons, switches, lights, thumbwheels and displays onto it and they move with it; select several parts and Put on a Panel (Ctrl+P) builds one around them. A panel has a style (enclosure door, flat plate, push-button station, operator console), a finish, a size and a title plate, and a Nameplate is an engraved legend such as START or HAND OFF AUTO. Panels and nameplates use no I/O points. In 3D the panel stands on a pedestal with the devices on its face.

Views

Top-down is the plan: lay the line out here. Side is the elevation, as the LogixPro simulator draws it: bottles stand on the belt and show their height, liquid, cap and crack, the fill tube comes down, the ram hits, tanks show their level. 3D is the shop floor: drag to orbit, wheel to zoom, right-drag or Shift+drag to pan, double-click a part to look at it, double-click the floor to see it all; with View → I/O Tags on Hover (3D) on, hovering a part shows its live I/O. All three are the same scene and the same I/O.

3D graphics

How much work the 3D view does is set under Theme → 3D graphics:

LevelWhat you get
HighMedium, plus ambient occlusion (the soft dark where a part meets the floor), a glow around lamps and lit lenses, and the finest shadows.
MediumTextured surfaces (concrete, belting, brushed metal), a sky over the outdoor scenes, sharp shadows around whatever the camera looks at, smoothed edges.
LowThe light renderer for phones and older PCs: one coarse shadow, no reflections, a painted halo instead of a real glow.
OffNo 3D view: Top-down and Side only.

Nothing about the machine changes with the level: the same parts, the same I/O, the same scan. The level starts from the graphics chip the browser reports until you pick one. If the 3D view runs slowly for a few seconds it steps down by itself (High to Medium, Medium to Low) and the status bar says so; 3D graphics: step down by itself when slow turns that off. Theme → 3D plant chooses the day or the night shift for the hall.

Watch for

A status-bar message that the graphics stepped down is the frame rate talking, not a fault. On a phone, leave 3D off while you write and test logic: Top-down and Side show every sensor and output, and they cost the battery almost nothing.

The machines as real machines

The parts are drawn as the equipment they stand for, and each one reports its own state on its own lamps, so you can read a machine off the floor without the tag monitor. None of this reaches the program: the same signals, the same tags, the same rungs.

A few things to read off them. The fill station’s sight glass drops a step with every large bottle and comes back with every refill, and LOW lights on its panel at 15 % before the program has said a word. The capper’s panel shows CAP, FEED, DOWN and LOW; the cap sorter’s disc turns one pocket for every cap pressed, so a chute running empty is visible from the top. The scrap and divert gates are pivot arms on an air cylinder whose reed switch, at the end of the stroke, is the Turned input: a rung that waits for Turned is waiting for that lamp. A clear pipe fills the first time liquid runs through it, and a soft shimmer moving along it means it is flowing now.

The Emitter is one of three real feeders, chosen in its Properties by what it feeds: a timing screw with a star wheel for filled bottles, an air conveyor on neck rails for empty PET, and a gravity magazine for cartons and metal parts. Each carries a beacon (READY, LOW, FAULT) and a screen. On AUTO the feeder runs while it has product and stops on a jam; tick Infeed signals to give the program Running, Low and Jam as inputs.

Try it: read the head tank off the machine

Run the bottle line in 3D and look at the fill station from the front. Every large bottle takes a step out of the sight glass, every refill from Supply_Tank puts it back. Stop the mix kitchen that feeds the supply tank and keep running: the level walks down, LOW lights at 15 % and the stack light goes from green to amber. Start the kitchen again and watch both come back.
